recipe.history:
The beet — Beta vulgaris — is among the oldest cultivated plants on earth, with a history stretching back more than four thousand years across the ancient Near East and Mediterranean. Wild sea beets grew along the coastlines of southern Europe and North Africa, and the ancient Babylonians, Greeks, and Romans all cultivated and ate the beet's large leaves long before they turned their attention to the swollen root beneath. The Greeks offered silver-shaped beets as tribute at the temple of Apollo at Delphi, valuing them highly enough to dedicate them to the god of sunlight and reason — which seems about right for a vegetable this brilliantly crimson. Beet cultivation for the root rather than purely the leaf became widespread through medieval Europe, particularly in Eastern Europe and Russia, where the earthy, hardy root thrived in cold soil and provided sustenance through brutal winters. Borscht — the iconic deep-red beet soup of Ukraine, Poland, and Russia — became one of the most enduring signatures of Eastern European cuisine, a testament to how deeply the beet embedded itself in the food culture of those regions. The golden beet, the Chioggia candy-stripe beet, and other heirloom varieties were developed through centuries of selective cultivation, each prized for distinct flavor profiles and visual beauty.

Beets made their complicated way into American cuisine through the canning industry of the late nineteenth century — pickled sliced beets in vinegar became an American diner staple and appeared on salad bars for decades, giving beets a somewhat unglamorous reputation as that thing in the can that stained everything it touched a violent magenta. The farm-to-table revolution of the late 1990s and 2000s rehabilitated the beet's image decisively, as chefs began roasting whole beets in foil, pickling them in house-made brine with spices, and shaving them raw over salads with goat cheese and walnuts. The beet's natural sweetness, amplified enormously by roasting, and its earthy mineral undertone made it a natural partner for rich beef. The first beet burgers to appear on serious menus weren't meat-substitute patties — they were real beef burgers topped with multiple preparations of beet at once, a testament to the vegetable's ability to behave as something more than a garnish.

I grew up with a grandmother who kept beets pickled in a large Ball jar in the back of the fridge at all times. I thought I hated them for most of my childhood because the only beets I knew were those cold, vinegar-soaked slices that bled purple into whatever they touched on the plate. My entire understanding of the beet was formed by that jar. Then, in my early twenties, a friend pulled whole beets wrapped in foil from a wood-fired oven and sliced them open at the table — and the steam that came off them smelled like soil and sweetness and some mineral depth I didn't have a word for. I ate them with salt and olive oil and understood for the first time that the beet I thought I knew was a completely different vegetable from the beet that was actually possible. I have been making up for lost time ever since.

Cooking a burger to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — matters especially in a burger of contrasting textures and temperatures like this one, where the toppings span the full range from raw to pickled to warm and roasted. The patty at medium rare is juicy enough to harmonize with the bright acidity of the pickled beets, earthy enough to meet the deep sweetness of the roasted beets, and assertive enough to hold its own against the crunch of the raw beet. A well-done patty in this context is simply dry and gray and defeated — it has already surrendered all the juice that would have created a conversation between the beef and the beet. The entire point of this burger is contrast and layering. That only works when the center of the equation — the patty — is exactly what it should be: pink, juicy, and alive at the correct temperature.
ingredients: For the pretzel bun bath and topping:
1 egg yolk beaten with 1 tablespoon water
Coarse pretzel salt or flaky sea salt
2 medium golden beets, peeled and sliced paper-thin on a mandoline
1 medium Chioggia (candy-stripe) beet, peeled and shaved paper-thin on a mandoline
6 slices sharp white cheddar (about 1 oz each)
instructions: 1. ROAST THE BEETS: Preheat oven to 400°F (205°C). Rub red beets with olive oil, salt, and pepper. Wrap individually in foil. Roast 50 to 60 minutes until a skewer pierces them with no resistance. Open foil and let cool 10 minutes. Slip skins off using paper towels. Slice into 1/4-inch rounds. Set aside.

2. PICKLE THE GOLDEN BEETS: Combine vinegar, water, sugar, salt, peppercorns, and thyme in a small saucepan. Bring to a boil, stir to dissolve sugar and salt. Pour hot brine over thinly sliced golden beets in a heatproof jar or bowl. Let sit at room temperature at least 1 hour, or refrigerate overnight for best results.
3. PREPARE THE RAW CHIOGGIA BEETS: Toss shaved Chioggia beet with olive oil, lemon juice, and a pinch of flaky salt just before assembly. Set aside.

4. MAKE THE PRETZEL BUNS: Combine yeast, warm water, and sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 to 8 minutes until foamy. Add flour, salt, and butter. Mix on low with the dough hook 2 minutes, then increase to medium and knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic.

5. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise at room temperature 1 to 1 1/2 hours until doubled. Punch down, divide into 6 equal portions, and shape into tight round balls. Place on parchment-lined baking sheets. Cover loosely and proof 45 minutes.

6. Preheat oven to 425°F (220°C). Bring 8 cups water with baking soda to a rolling boil in a wide pot. Working in batches, gently lower buns into the boiling baking soda bath using a slotted spoon. Boil 30 seconds per side. Return to parchment-lined baking sheet.
7. Brush boiled buns with egg yolk wash. Sprinkle with coarse pretzel salt. Bake 14 to 16 minutes until deep mahogany brown. Cool on a wire rack.
8. MAKE THE HORSERADISH CRÈME FRAÎCHE: Stir together crème fraîche, horseradish, lemon juice, chives, and salt in a small bowl. Taste and adjust horseradish to preference. Refrigerate until needed.

9. FORM THE PATTIES: Gently combine ground chuck and ground short rib. Season with salt and pepper. Form into 6 patties, 4 1/2 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.
10. COOK THE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties without pressing, 3 minutes on the first side until a deep crust forms.

11. Flip once. Lay a slice of white cheddar over each patty. Cook 2 to 2 1/2 minutes more. Check internal temperature — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Transfer to a wire rack and rest 3 minutes.
12. TOAST THE BUNS: Split pretzel buns and toast cut-side down in a hot dry skillet 60 to 90 seconds.
13. DRESS THE ARUGULA: Toss baby arugula with olive oil, lemon juice, and a pinch of salt just before assembly.
14. ASSEMBLE: Spread horseradish crème fraîche generously on both cut sides of the pretzel bun. Place a small handful of dressed arugula on the bottom bun. Add the rested, cheese-topped patty.
15. Layer roasted red beet slices over the patty. Add several slices of pickled golden beet. Finish with a small crown of raw Chioggia beet shavings.
16. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
